quickAnswer.question: How do I get a transcript of a Facebook video?
quickAnswer.answer: Copy the link to a public Facebook video and paste it into TranscriptX. It pulls the audio and produces the full transcript within seconds, across more than 100 languages, ready for you to read, copy, edit or export. You do not need to sign up, and there is nothing to install.

content: A Facebook transcript is the spoken content of a Facebook video written out as text. Everything said in the clip — a Live host answering questions, a creator narrating a Reel, a speaker in a recorded event — becomes words you can read, search and copy instead of scrubbing back and forth through the video.

Facebook is a hard place to get information back out of. Videos are scattered across your feed, inside groups, on Pages, and in old Live broadcasts that can be an hour long, and the platform gives you no clean way to read what was said. A transcript solves that: it turns a buried, unsearchable video into text you can actually work with.

This page exists to do one thing well — get the words out of a Facebook video. Whether you think of it as getting the transcript, generating one with AI, or converting the video to text, the result is the same, so it all lives on a single tool rather than being split across duplicates.
TranscriptX generates the transcript free, in the browser, with no account required.

sections.h2: How to Get a Transcript From a Facebook Video

steps.content: Open the video on Facebook, click the three-dot menu or the timestamp, and copy the link — or copy the URL from the address bar on desktop. The video needs to be public.
Drop the link into the box above. There is no account to create and nothing to upload; the tool reads the video straight from the link.
TranscriptX listens to the audio, detects the spoken language on its own across more than 100 languages, separates each speaker, and writes the words out with punctuation.
Read it on screen, copy the whole thing or a single quote, edit it, translate it, or download it to keep.

sections.h2: A Facebook Transcript Generator That Works Without Captions
content: Most Facebook videos have no reliable caption track to pull from, and the auto-captions that do appear are often incomplete or wrong. So TranscriptX works as a Facebook transcript generator: it builds the text from the audio itself rather than depending on captions the creator may never have added.

That means you can transcribe Facebook video audio even when there is nothing on screen to copy — and transcribe a Facebook video that only ever went out as a Live. The AI-powered generator handles a single narrator, a two-person interview, or a room full of voices on a recorded Live, labelling each speaker as it goes. Because this Facebook transcript AI works from the audio, the result is usually cleaner than Facebook's own captions, especially on accents and specialist vocabulary.
Facebook video transcription runs the same way in every language it hears — a Live in Spanish or a Reel in Tagalog comes back as text in that language, detected automatically.

If you do not think in terms of the word transcript and simply want to turn a Facebook video to text, this is the same tool under a name that fits. Drop in the link, and everything spoken in the video returns as clean, readable text.

Turning a Facebook video to text is useful well beyond reading it once. A recorded Live becomes a document you can search for the one answer you needed, a long community meeting becomes minutes you can share with people who missed it, and a creator's video becomes source material you can quote or repurpose — all from the text rather than the timeline.

sections.h2: What You Can Transcribe on Facebook
intro: Facebook holds more kinds of video than most platforms, and a transcript helps with all of them. The most common ones people convert:

items.content: Live broadcasts are often the longest and most information-dense videos on Facebook — webinars, Q&As, sermons, class sessions, community meetings. A transcript turns an hour of Live into text you can read in minutes and search for the part that mattered.
A talking-head update, an announcement or an explainer posted to a feed becomes quotable, searchable text instead of a clip you have to replay to reference.
Short-form Facebook Reels move fast, and the useful part is often a single line. A transcript captures it as text before it scrolls out of the feed.
Educational content, tutorials and discussions posted inside groups or on Pages turn into notes and references you can keep outside the platform.
Panels, talks and interviews streamed or posted on Facebook become transcripts with each speaker labelled, so you can pull an exact quote and attribute it correctly.

content: Once the transcript is on screen it is yours to use however the next step needs. Copy the whole thing or just one quote, edit the text to fix a name or trim filler, or translate it into another language without leaving the page.

When you want it saved rather than on screen, export it as TXT, DOCX, PDF, SRT or VTT — plain text for reading and pasting, a document for editing, a fixed file for sharing, or a timed caption file if the video needs subtitles.

Working across platforms too? The [YouTube Transcript](/youtube-transcript) and [TikTok Transcript](/tiktok-transcript) tools do the same job for those sites, and if your source is an audio file rather than a video, the [Audio to Text](/audio-to-text) tool is built for that.

How closely the transcript matches the video depends mostly on the audio. A clear speaker in a well-recorded Live or a scripted Reel comes back close to word for word, while a noisy room, people talking over each other, or a weak phone-recorded stream will need more review.

The passages worth checking are the usual ones — names, numbers, and any technical or specialist terms — which take seconds to fix against the video compared with transcribing the whole thing yourself.

TranscriptX recognises speech in over 100 languages and detects which one it is hearing automatically, so a Facebook video in any language comes back as a transcript in that same language, with speakers kept separate throughout.
